subject: music
source_note: Topic structure follows the National Curriculum KS3 programme of study for music. Connections, sequence and prerequisites are expert-authored teaching relationships.

units.name: Performing
units.blurb: Singing and playing instruments in solo and ensemble contexts

units.name: Composing
units.blurb: Improvising and composing across structures, styles and traditions

units.name: Notation & the Elements of Music
units.blurb: Reading notation and using the interrelated dimensions of music

units.name: Listening & Understanding
units.blurb: Listening to a wide range of music and understanding its history

topics.name: Performing Skills
topics.blurb: Playing fluently and with accuracy and expression on voice and instruments

topics.name: Solo & Ensemble
topics.blurb: Performing confidently in solo and group contexts

topics.name: Improvising & Composing
topics.blurb: Generating and shaping original musical ideas

topics.name: Developing Musical Ideas
topics.blurb: Extending ideas across structures, styles, genres and traditions

topics.name: Staff & Other Notation
topics.blurb: Reading and using staff and other relevant notations accurately

topics.name: Dimensions of Music
topics.blurb: Using pitch, rhythm, tonalities, scales and other devices expressively

topics.name: Listening to Great Music
topics.blurb: Listening with discrimination to music from great composers and musicians

topics.name: Understanding Music & its History
topics.blurb: Deepening understanding of musical styles, traditions and history

connections.why: Secure individual technique is what makes confident ensemble playing possible
Expressive performance depends on controlling the dimensions of music
Reading notation lets performers realise written music accurately
Notation is how composers record and communicate their ideas
Composing means manipulating pitch, rhythm, tonality and other dimensions
Initial ideas are extended and developed into fuller compositions
Hearing how great composers develop ideas models the craft for pupils
Discriminating listening builds understanding of styles and their history
Knowledge of styles, genres and traditions feeds pupils' own composing
Identifying the dimensions of music sharpens what pupils hear
Group music-making is a natural setting for improvisation
Understanding a style's conventions informs how it should be performed
